DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
LOCAL PANEL
On May 7, 2025, Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) Anna Hamburg-Gal issued a
Recommended Decision and Order (“RDO”) recommending the dismissal of the majority interest
petition filed by Petitioner Chicago Fire Fighters Union, Local 2, IAFF (“Union”), which seeks to
include employees in the titles Deputy District Chief (“DDC”) and Assistant Deputy Chief
Paramedic1 to its historical unit of uniformed members of Respondent City of Chicago, Fire
Department (“Employer”). The ALJ recommended dismissal of the Petition, finding that the DDCs
are above the highest-ranking company officer and thus, are supervisory employees within the
meaning of Section 3(r) of the Act. The ALJ further found that, should the Board determine that the
DDCs are not above the highest-ranking company officer, none of the DDCs satisfied the four-part
supervisory test. She also determined that certain of the DDCs were not managerial employees and
that certain others fell within the managerial and confidential employee exclusions.
Petitioner filed exceptions challenging the ALJ’s determinations and conclusions resulting in
the recommendation to dismiss the Petition.2 Specifically, Petitioner takes exception to the ALJ’s
1 On February 6, 2024, Petitioner withdrew its petition with respect to the Assistant Deputy Chief Paramedic title.
2 On June 12, 2025, we granted Petitioner leave to file its exceptions instanter.
1

determinations on the company office issue, her findings that the DDCs exercise supervisory
authority with independent judgment, and determination that DDC Mark Kiely is a managerial
employee excluded from the Act’s coverage. The City filed responses to Petitioner’s exceptions and
cross-exceptions to the ALJ’s alternative findings that the DDCs are not supervisors under the four-
part supervisory test and her determinations regarding the managerial employee exclusion, to which
Petitioner filed cross-responses.3 Due to the significance and novelty of the company officer issue
and upon Petitioner’s request, the matter was scheduled for oral argument, which was held at the
Board’s October 23, 2025 meeting.
Upon consideration of the record, the RDO, the exceptions, responses thereto, supporting
briefs, and the parties’ oral arguments, we find as follows:
3 On June 23, 2025, Respondent timely filed responses to Petitioner’s exceptions and also filed cross-exceptions.
Petitioner then filed a document titled “Petitioner’s Cross-Responses and Reply to Employer’s Response to Union’s
Exceptions and Cross-Exceptions to Administrative Law Judge’s Recommended Decision and Order” (“Petitioner’s
Cross-Responses”). This last submission triggered the following procedural motions, responses, and replies, as titled by
the respective party: (1) Respondent’s Motion to Strike Portions of Petitioner’s Cross-Response and Reply
(“Respondent’s Motion to Strike Reply”); (2) Petitioner’s Response to Employer’s Motion to Strike Portions of
Petitioner’s Cross-Response and Reply and Cross-Motion to Strike (“Petitioner’s Response to Motion to Strike 1”); (3)
Respondent’s Response to Petitioner’s Request for Variance, in the Alternative (“Response to Request for Variance”);
(4) Petitioner’s Reply to Respondent’s Response to Request for Variance in the Alternative (“Reply to Response to
Request for Variance”); and (5) Respondent’s email moving to strike Petitioner’s Reply to Respondent’s Response to
Request for Variance in the Alternative (“Respondent’s Motion to Strike Reply 2”).
On August 14, 2025, we granted, in part, Respondent’s Motion to Strike Reply 1, and denied Petitioner’s request
for a variance. Respondent’s Motion to Strike Reply 1 was granted to the extent that Section II.A of Petitioner’s Cross
Responses was stricken as a reply to Respondent’s response to Petitioner’s exceptions. Section II.A, pages 2-9, of
Petitioner’s Cross-Responses is tantamount to a reply to Respondent’s response to Petitioner’s exceptions. That section
specifically references arguments contained in Respondent’s responses to Petitioner’s exceptions and cannot be read to
serve any other purpose than as a reply to Respondent’s responses to Petitioner’s exceptions to the RDO. The first
paragraph of Section II.A. begins by asserting that the “City erroneously argues that that the ALJ correctly found that the
Deputy District Chiefs (“DDC”) are supervisors within the meaning of the Act because they hold a rank above that of
the highest company officer” citing a page from Respondent’s response to Petitioner’s exceptions. (Petitioner’s Cross-
Response, p. 2). The remainder of that section is replete with argument related to Respondent’s response to Petitioner’s
exceptions to the ALJ’s determinations regarding the company officer issue. The Board’s rules do not provide for replies
to responses to exceptions or appeals. See 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135. As Respondent observes, recently, and under
similar circumstances, the Board’s State Panel struck a party’s reply to the opposing party’s response to exceptions that
was filed without leave to do so. See., e.g., Univ. Park Prof’l Fire Fighters Ass’n, 41 PERI ¶ 146 (IL LRB-SP 2025)
(striking a reply to response to exceptions filed without leave or a variance from the Board’s rules). Here, Petitioner
neither moved for leave to file a reply nor requested a variance from the Board’s rules before filing the reply.
2

Company Officer Issue
The key issue in this case is whether the DDCs qualify as company officers. The ALJ
determined that, in the event we determine that they are the highest rank of company officers, the
DDCs are not supervisors under the four-part supervisory test found in the first paragraph of Section
3(r)(1) of the Act. Resolving the company officer issue involves interpretation of language in the
second paragraph of Section 3(r)(1), amended by Public Act 102–686 (P.A. 102-686, eff. June 1,
2022) (“2022 Amendment”). The second paragraph of Section 3(r)(1) states as follows:
Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding paragraph, in
determining supervisory status in fire fighter employment, no fire fighter
shall be excluded as a supervisor who has established representation rights
under Section 9 of this Act. Further, in new fire fighter units, employees
shall consist of fire fighters of the highest rank of company officer and
below. A company officer may be responsible for multiple companies
or apparatus on a shift, multiple stations, or an entire shift. There may
be more than one company officer per shift. If a company officer
otherwise qualifies as a supervisor under the preceding paragraph,
however, he or she shall not be included in the fire fighter unit. If there is
no rank between that of chief and the highest company officer, the employer
may designate a position on each shift as a Shift Commander, and the
persons occupying those positions shall be supervisors. All other ranks
above that of the highest company officer shall be supervisors.”
5 ILCS 315/3(r)(1). (Relevant changes noted by strikethrough text and bolded underline).
The ALJ found that the plain meaning and legislative history of the 2022 Amendment did not
change or expand the definition of “company officer” established by Board and court precedents,
which hold that “company officer” refers to an employee who oversees a company, i.e., personnel
assigned to a vehicle, equipment, or ambulance. See City of Freeport v. Ill. State Labor Relations
Bd., 135 Ill.2d 499, 522 (1990); Vill. of Elk Grove Vill. v. Ill. State Labor Relations Bd., 245 Ill.
App. 3d 109, 211 (2d Dist. 1993); City of Evanston, 5 PERI ¶ 2023, fn. 6 (IL SLRB 1989). The ALJ
noted that the legislative discussion of the 2022 Amendment implicitly affirmed the Board’s decision
in Village of Palatine, 25 PERI ¶ 114 (IL LRB-SP 2009), where the Board included the Village of
3

Palatine’s captains in the existing bargaining unit as company officers because they functioned as
company officers “no differently” than the lieutenants who had immediate responsibility for
personnel assigned to one or more companies. Id. She then concluded that the DDCs are above the
highest rank of company officer.
Petitioner’s Exceptions and Employer’s Response
Petitioner takes exception to the ALJ’s determinations on the company office issue,
contending that the ALJ erred in concluding that the DDCs are above the highest rank of company
officer. Petitioner focuses on the following language of the 2022 Amendment: “A company officer
may be responsible for multiple companies or apparatus on a shift, multiple stations, or an
entire shift. There may be more than one company officer per shift.” It contends that this
language expands the definition of company officers to include those employees who “may be
responsible” for more than one company or apparatus on a shift, one station, or for an entire shift. In
addition to Village of Palatine, 25 PERI ¶ 114 ( ILRB-SP 2009), the Union contends that the 2022
Amendment was passed in response to City of Rolling Meadows, 34 PERI ¶ 81 (ILRB-SP G.C. Order,
Oct. 14, 2017), in which a Board ALJ excluded Battalion Chiefs because they held a rank above that
of the lieutenants who served as company officers. In support of its claim that the intent of the 2022
Amendment was to include those officers in ranks that were responsible for more than one crew or
apparatus, Petitioner points to the ALJ’s finding there that the lieutenants’ connection to a single
apparatus or crew is determinative of company officer status. In the instant case, Petitioner asserts
that the DDCs who are responsible for multiple companies, apparatus on a shift, stations, and the
entire shift in their respective districts, satisfy this expanded definition of company officer. The
Petitioner further asserts that the DDCs share these responsibilities with their subordinate Battalion
Chiefs.
4

The Employer responds that the ALJ correctly analyzed the language of the 2022 Amendment
and its legislative history in finding that the DDCs are above the highest-ranking company officer. It
asserts that the evidence, including testimony from the DDCs, failed to demonstrate that the DDCs
serve as company officers, so the DDCs cannot be the highest-ranking company officers. The
Employer contends that the 2022 Amendment did not remove or change the meaning of company
officer as defined in previous Board rulings and caselaw. The 2022 Amendment merely clarified that
that “company officers” may include individuals like the captains in Village of Palatine and did not
provide a “new definition” of company officer. Furthermore, the Employer points out that the
Department does not consider the DDCs to be company officers and the DDCs do not consider
themselves to be company officers. Finally, the Employer contends that Petitioner failed to take
exception to the ALJ’s findings on the highest rank immediately responsible for crew on the fire side
and on the EMS side of the department, and thus, has waived its right to do so.4
We find merit to Petitioner’s exceptions to the ALJ’s findings and determinations on the
company officer issue. In finding that the DDCs are above the highest ranking company officer, the
ALJ took the approach that the amendatory language “may be responsible for multiple companies or
apparatus on a shift, multiple stations, or an entire shift” was intended to “convey that these were
potential functions of a company officer rather than proof of company officer status,” and that the
plain language “preserved the existing definitions of “companies” and “company officer” established
by the courts and the Board rather than rejecting the common understanding of that term used in
previous decisions.
4 We find that Petitioner did not waive its right to take exception to the ALJ’s findings on the highest rank immediately
responsible for crew on the fire side and on the EMS side of the department. We find that Petitioner’s exception to the
ALJ’s finding that the DDCs occupy a rank above that of the highest rank of company officer effectively disputes the
ALJ’s findings in question.
5

We find, however, that the amendatory language used by the legislature expresses the intent
to broaden the definition of “company officer” to include those employees, in this case the DDCs,
who are “responsible for multiple companies or apparatus on a shift, multiple stations, or an entire
shift” without necessarily finding that the amendment rejects the common understanding of company
officer to mean the employee responsible for a single company or crew.
The ALJ found support for her interpretation of the express language in the legislative history
of the 2022 Amendment, citing a portion of Representative Lawrence Walsh’s opening statement in
support of House Bill 220, in which he stated:
By adding this language that the company officer may be responsible
for the things mentioned above, it basically is changing the definition
of what a company officer is and clarifying that and going along with
the ruling from the Illinois Labor Relations Board
Illinois House Transcript, 2021 Reg. Sess. No. 19, at pp. 53-54. The ALJ noted that the legislative
discussion of the 2022 Amendment supports the interpretation of the language as clarifying rather
than rejecting the common understanding of the term “company officer.” Although Rep. Walsh did
not identify the “ruling from the Illinois Labor Relations Board” to which he was referring, the ALJ
found an implicit reference to the Board’s decision in Village of Palatine. The ALJ observed that
implicit in the Board’s determination that the Village of Palatine’s captains were company officers,
was the captains’ “immediate responsibility of the personnel of one or more crews (engines and
ambulances) either by virtue of being ‘in charge of’ a station that was comprised of those crews or
by being ‘in charge of’ the crew on a particular piece of equipment at an incident.” (RDO, p. 42).
We disagree with the ALJ’s interpretation of the amendatory language. The 2022 Amendment
does not use the word “immediate” or “immediately” to qualify how a company officer “may be
responsible for multiple companies or apparatus on a shift, multiple stations, or an entire shift, and
the word “immediate” or “immediately” does not appear in the legislative discussions in describing
6

such responsibilities. Had the legislature intended to limit the company officer designation to those
employees who had “immediate” responsibility for multiple companies or apparatus on a shift,
multiple stations, or an entire shift, it could have used “immediately” to describe “may be responsible
for” in amending Section 3(r)(1). But the legislature did not do so, and we decline to read into the
plain language of the amendment terms or limitations not expressed by the legislature in amending
the statute. Petersen v. Wallach, 198 Ill. 2d 439, 446 (2002).
Our interpretation of the express language is consistent with the purposes and policies of the
Act, construing the amended supervisory exclusion in Section 3(r)(1) to extend collective bargaining
rights broadly. See City of Decatur v. Am. Fed’n of State, Cnty., & Mun. Emps., Local 268, 122 Ill.
2d 353 (1988). It also finds support in the legislative discussions. Representative Walsh notes that
HB 220 was initiated by the IAFF “in response” to a decision from the Board. It is likely that the
decision to which he was referring is the non-precedential final order in City of Rolling Meadows,
34 PERI ¶ 81, issued in 2017 and closer in time to the 2022 Amendment, which was not favorable to
unions seeking to include employees in firefighter units because company officer status was limited
to responsibility for just one company or crew, rather than the Board’s decision in Village of Palatine,
issued in 2009, that found in favor of the petitioning union where the number of companies was not
expressly determinative. As noted above, in City of Rolling Meadows, the ALJ found the lieutenants’
connection to a single apparatus or crew determinative of company officer status in excluding
Battalion Chiefs who the ALJ observed “are never directly tied to just one crew or apparatus.” City
of Rolling Meadows, 34 PERI 81. In Village of Palatine, however, the Board found the captains in
that case to be company officers because they were responsible for one station or company nearly as
often as the lieutenants who were considered company officers. Vill. of Palatine, 25 PERI ¶ 114.
7

Accordingly, we reject the ALJ’s findings and recommendations on the company officer issue
and find that the DDCs are company officers under the express language of Section 3(r)(1) of the
Act.
Supervisory and Managerial Exclusions
The ALJ noted that should we find that the DDCs are not above the highest rank of company
officer, she would find that none of the DDCs satisfy the four-part supervisory test. The ALJ observed
that although the principal work of the DDCs is obviously and visibly different from that of their
subordinates and they exercise certain supervisory authority with independent judgment when
performing particular job duties, none of the DDCs spend a preponderance of their time exercising
supervisory authority under either a quantitative or qualitative test.
Next the ALJ determined that the Special Operations DDCs Jason Lach, Douglas Schick, and
Davide Doggett, Training Division DDC Richard Stack, and Fire Prevention DDC Evan Person are
not managerial employees within the meaning of the Act. She observed that none of these petitioned-
for employees predominantly engaged in executive and managerial functions or are responsible for
effectuating management policies and practices. The ALJ did, however, conclude that the DDC for
the Mobile Reporting Unit (“MRU”), Mark Kiely, should be excluded as a managerial employee
under Section 3(j) of the Act.
We reject as meritless, Petitioner’s exceptions to the ALJ’s findings regarding the 4-part
supervisory test and managerial employee test as well as the Employer’s cross-exceptions and accept
the ALJ’s alternative findings and recommendations that the DDCs are not supervisors under the 4-
part supervisory test. In addition, we accept the ALJs’ recommendations regarding managerial status
for the employees and positions listed on page 85 of the RDO.
8

For the above reasons, we reject the ALJ’s recommendations regarding the company officer
issue and find that the DDCs are company officers within the meaning of Section 3(r)(1) of the Act.
In addition, we accept the ALJ’s recommendations that the DDCs are not supervisors under the 4-
part supervisory test of Section 3(r) of the Act and that certain DDCs are not managerial employees
under Section 3(j) of the Act. Finally, we accept the ALJ’s recommendations that DDC Mark Kiely
is a managerial employee excluded from collective bargaining under Section 3(j) of the Act and that
the position of DDC – Manpower Division is excluded from bargaining as confidential under Section
3(c) of the Act.
We direct the Executive Director to certify Petitioner as the exclusive representative of the
bargaining unit as described in the Petition and consistent with the findings set forth in this Decision
and Order.
BY THE LOCAL PANEL OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
